parts.problem_md: Evaluate whether a joint venture is the best way for a business to enter a new international market.
parts.solution_md:
A joint venture is an agreement in which two businesses set up a separate business together and share its costs, risks and profits **[K]**. Entering a new international market is expensive and risky, because a business may not understand local tastes, laws or distribution systems. A food manufacturer moving into a country where religious rules affect which ingredients are acceptable **[Ap]** could take years to learn this on its own. Working with a partner already established there gives the business that knowledge immediately, and the set-up costs are shared, so expansion becomes possible for a business that could not afford to enter the market by itself **[An]**

However, a joint venture also means giving up control **[K]**. Every major decision must be agreed with the partner, and the two businesses may want different things - one may want rapid growth while the other prefers steady profits **[Ap]**. Disagreements can slow decisions down at exactly the moment a new market needs a quick response to competitors, and any profit made has to be shared rather than kept in full **[An]**

Whether a joint venture is the best method depends on the circumstances **[E]**. Where the market is very different from the home market, or where a government requires foreign firms to work with a local partner, a joint venture may be the only realistic way in **[E]**. Where the business already understands the market and has enough finance, setting up its own operation would let it keep full control and all of the profit, which is likely to be better over time **[E]**. Much also depends on how well matched the partners are, since a joint venture between firms with similar aims is far more likely to work than one formed simply because a partner was available **[E]**. Overall, a joint venture is the best choice when risk and unfamiliarity are high, rather than in every case **[E]**

However, profits are divided in the same proportion, so a successful venture returns less than a wholly owned operation would
> - A local partner brings knowledge that would otherwise take years and considerable expense to acquire, including established supplier and distributor relationships, consumer preferences, and familiarity with local employment and product regulations, shortening the time before the business earns revenue. However, sharing designs, technology or commercial knowledge carries the risk that the partner later becomes a competitor using what it has learned
> - Some governments restrict foreign ownership and require overseas firms to operate through a joint venture with a domestic company, so the choice becomes one between a joint venture and staying out of the market altogether rather than between a joint venture and a wholly owned subsidiary. However, where no such rule applies, a business with sufficient finance and market knowledge may do better setting up alone
> - Each partner can contribute what it does best, one providing brand recognition and product technology while the other provides manufacturing capacity and distribution, which may produce a stronger entry than either could achieve independently. However, control is shared, so decisions on pricing, marketing and reinvestment must be agreed, and disagreement slows response at exactly the point a new market demands speed
> - The business could instead enter by exporting, licensing, franchising or setting up a wholly owned subsidiary, each carrying a different balance of risk, control and commitment. However, the lower-risk options generally give less control over how the product is presented, while the higher-control options require considerably more capital and local knowledge
> 
> Accept any other valid response

parts.problem_md:
> **[case-study]**
> **Spoke (SP)**
> 
> Spoke (SP) is a workers' co-operative in country V. It sells and repairs bicycles from six shops in and around the capital city.
> 
> SP was formed nine years ago. Its founder was retiring and had no family willing to take over the business, so he sold it to the people who worked there. Today all 48 employees are members of the co-operative. Each member owns an equal share, has one vote at members' meetings, and receives a share of any surplus the business makes at the end of the year.
> 
> **Table 1.1: SP selected data**
> 
> | Members (employee-owners) | 48 |
> |---|---|
> | Shops | 6 |
> | Revenue in 2025 (\$) | 3,400,000 |
> | Surplus shared among members in 2025 (\$) | 210,000 |
> | Labour turnover at SP (%) | 6 |
> | Average labour turnover, bicycle retail in country V (%) | 19 |
> 
> Two national bicycle chains have opened branches in the capital city in the past three years. Both sell at lower prices than SP, but neither offers a repair service. SP's members believe their reputation for skilled repair work is what keeps customers returning.
> 
> SP's members have been discussing whether to open a seventh shop, which would cost around \$140,000. Because SP cannot sell shares to outside investors, the money would have to come from surpluses the members would otherwise share between themselves. At the last members' meeting the proposal was postponed for a year.

Analyse **two** advantages to SP of operating as a co-operative.
parts.solution_md:
One advantage is that members are motivated because they share in the surplus the business makes **[K]**. All 48 of SP's employees own an equal part of the co-operative and shared \$210,000 between them in 2025 **[Ap]**. Because every member gains directly when SP does well, they have a strong reason to work carefully and to look for ways of serving customers better, rather than doing only the minimum their job requires **[An]**. This helps explain why labour turnover at SP is just 6% against an industry average of 19%, which means SP keeps its experienced repair staff and avoids the cost of constantly recruiting and training replacements **[An]** A second advantage is that each member has an equal vote in how SP is run **[K]**. Decisions such as which bicycles to stock, or whether to spend \$140,000 on a seventh shop, are therefore taken by the mechanics and shop staff who serve customers every day **[Ap]**. These members know which repairs are requested most often and which models cause problems, so SP is likely to choose its stock more accurately than a business where such decisions are made by managers with no direct contact with customers **[An]**. Members are also more willing to accept difficult decisions, such as postponing the new shop for a year, because they voted on them themselves, so SP avoids the resentment and falling effort that such a decision might cause elsewhere **[An]** > **[mark-scheme]** > - An 8-mark analyse question requires two developed points, each with knowledge of a relevant concept, applied to the business context, and followed by a chain of reasoning that explains the causes, impacts or consequences for the business > - This is a 'Level of response' answer where the examiner judges how well you have displayed the key skills of knowledge, application and analysis > > | **Level** | **Knowledge** | **Application** | **Analysis** | > |---|---|---|---| > | **2** | **2 marks**

> **[case-study]**
> **Anvil (AV)**
> 
> Anvil (AV) is a private limited company in country W. It has manufactured metal components for washing machines and refrigerators since 1974 and employs 90 people at a single factory.
> 
> Country W's economy has changed considerably. Manufacturing has declined as appliance makers have moved production to countries where wages are lower, while banking, tourism and software have grown quickly. Table 1.1 shows how the economic sectors have changed.
> 
> **Table 1.1: Share of country W's national output by sector**
> 
> |   | **2010** | **2025** |
> |---|---|---|
> | Primary sector (%) | 18 | 16 |
> | Secondary sector (%) | 34 | 21 |
> | Tertiary sector (%) | 48 | 63 |
> 
> Six of the appliance manufacturers that AV supplied in 2010 have since closed their factories in country W or moved them overseas.
> 
> **Table 1.2: AV selected data**
> 
> | Revenue in 2020 (\$m) | 6.2 |
> |---|---|
> | Revenue in 2025 (\$m) | 4.1 |
> | Average age of production workers | 49 |
> | Applications per skilled machinist vacancy, 2015 | 11 |
> | Applications per skilled machinist vacancy, 2025 | 2 |
> 
> AV's Operations Director notes that school leavers in country W increasingly train for work in offices, hotels and software firms rather than factories.
> 
> AV's directors are considering whether the business should begin servicing and repairing domestic appliances, rather than only manufacturing the parts that go into them.

Analyse **two** consequences for AV of the changing relative importance of the economic sectors in country W.
parts.solution_md:
One consequence is that AV faces falling demand from its domestic customers **[K]**. The secondary sector has shrunk from 34% to 21% of country W's output since 2010, and six of the appliance manufacturers AV supplied have closed or moved abroad **[Ap]**. Because AV sells components to these manufacturers rather than to the public, every factory that leaves country W removes a customer permanently, which helps explain why AV's revenue has fallen from \$6.2m to \$4.1m in only five years **[An]**. If this decline continues, AV will not have enough orders to keep its factory working at a level that covers its fixed costs, which is why its directors are now considering moving into appliance servicing instead **[An]** A second consequence is that AV finds it much harder to recruit skilled workers **[K]**. As the tertiary sector has grown from 48% to 63% of national output, school leavers are training for office, hotel and software work instead, and AV now receives only two applications for each skilled machinist vacancy compared with eleven in 2015 **[Ap]**. With the average age of its production workers at 49, AV is likely to lose experienced staff to retirement faster than it can replace them **[An]**. parts.problem_md: Explain **two **disadvantages to a private limited company of changing to a public limited company.
parts.solution_md:
One disadvantage is that the original owners lose control of the business **[1]**. Once shares are freely available on the stock exchange, any member of the public can buy them without needing approval from existing shareholders and could outvote the founders on key decisions **[1]**

There is also a significantly higher risk of takeover **[1]**. Because shares can be freely bought and sold on the stock exchange, a rival company or investor could gradually acquire enough shares to gain control of the business entirely **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Explain requires a clear statement of meaning (AO1) supported by contextual development (AO2)
> 
> - Valid AO1 is awarded 2 marks
> - Valid AO2 is awarded up to 2 marks
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> AO1
> 
> - High cost of preparing documentation and floating the company on the stock exchange
> - Any member of the public can purchase shares without needing approval from existing shareholders
> - Higher public profile means business problems are more visible and may attract greater media scrutiny
> - Divorce of ownership and control — original owners lose total control over the direction of the business
> - Higher risk of takeover by an outside individual or business
> 
> AO2
> 
> - The cost of floating can be substantial, diverting money away from investment in the business at a critical time
> - Without control over who buys shares, the original owners could find themselves outvoted on key decisions by new shareholders whose interests differ from their own
> - Greater public scrutiny means any negative news, poor financial results or controversies are more likely to become widely known, damaging the company's reputation
> - With ownership and control separated, professional managers may make decisions that conflict with the founders' original vision or values for the business
> - Once shares are freely traded on the stock exchange, a rival company or investor could acquire enough shares to take over the business against the wishes of the original owners
> 
> Other valid chains of reasoning are acceptable.

parts.problem_md: Explain **two **advantages that a business in the public sector may have that a business in the private sector may not.
parts.solution_md:
One advantage of being in the public sector is easier access to finance, as the business is funded by the government through taxation **[1]**. This means it does not need to attract private investors or take on commercial loans **[1]**

A second advantage is that public sector businesses are not under pressure to make a profit **[1]**. This means they can focus on providing essential services to all customers, including those in areas or situations that a private sector business would consider unprofitable **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Explain requires a clear statement of meaning (AO1) supported by contextual development (AO2)
> 
> - Valid AO1 is awarded 2 marks
> - Valid AO2 is awarded up to 2 marks
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> AO1
> 
> - Easier access to finance as the business is funded by the government
> - Not under pressure to make a profit, as it often provides essential goods or services
> - Does not have to pay dividends to shareholders
> - Often a large business that can benefit from economies of scale
> 
> AO2
> 
> - Government funding means finance can be raised through taxation or grants, without needing to attract private investors or take on commercial loans
> - Without the need to make a profit, the business can focus on providing quality services to all customers, including those in unprofitable areas that a private business would not serve
> - Not paying dividends means any surplus can be reinvested into improving services rather than being distributed to shareholders
> - Economies of scale allow the business to produce goods or services at a lower average cost, meaning it can offer better value than many private sector competitors
> 
> Other valid chains of reasoning are acceptable.

parts.problem_md: Explain **two **limitations of partnership as a business structure.
parts.solution_md:
One limitation of a partnership is that all partners have unlimited liability, meaning their personal assets - such as their home or savings - could be used to pay business debts if the partnership fails **[1]**. This is a significant risk, as each partner is liable for the debts of the whole business, not just their own share **[1]**

A second limitation is that all partners are legally bound by the decisions of any one partner **[1]**. This means that if one partner makes a poor business decision - such as signing an expensive contract - the other partners are responsible for the consequences **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Explain requires a clear statement of meaning (AO1) supported by contextual development (AO2)
> 
> - Valid AO1 is awarded 2 marks
> - Valid AO2 is awarded up to 2 marks
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> AO1
> 
> - All partners have unlimited liability
> - Profits must be shared between partners
> - All partners share losses
> - All partners are bound by the decisions of any one partner
> - Compromises are necessary in decision-making, which can lead to conflict
> - Ability to raise capital is limited, as partnerships cannot sell shares
> - Continuity is not assured - the partnership must be reformed if a partner dies or leaves
> 
> AO2
> 
> - Unlimited liability means all personal assets - including savings and property - are at risk if the business cannot pay its debts
> - Sharing profits means each partner receives less than they would as a sole trader generating the same revenue
> - Each partner is personally responsible for losses, including those caused by the decisions of other partners
> - One partner's poor decisions bind all others, meaning the actions of a single partner could cause financial harm to the whole business without the others' agreement
> - Disagreements between partners can slow down decision-making or lead to poor compromises that damage the business
> - The inability to sell shares makes it harder to raise large amounts of finance compared to a limited company, restricting growth
> - If a partner dies or leaves, the partnership must be legally reformed, causing disruption to the business
> 
> Other valid chains of reasoning are acceptable.

parts.problem_md: Explain **two **advantages to a business of buying a franchise.
parts.solution_md:
One advantage of buying a franchise is that the franchisee benefits from the franchisor's established brand and reputation **[1]**. Customers already know and trust the product, making it easier to attract sales from day one **[1]**

A second advantage is that marketing and advertising costs are shared across all franchisees **[1]**. This means the individual franchisee spends less on promotion while still benefiting from national or wider campaigns **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Explain requires a clear statement of meaning (AO1) supported by contextual development (AO2)
> 
> - Valid AO1 is awarded 2 marks
> - Valid AO2 is awarded up to 2 marks
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> AO1
> 
> - The franchisee benefits from the established reputation and brand of the franchisor
> - Marketing and advertising costs are shared across all franchisees
> - Help and advice is available from the franchisor
> - The product or service is already known by customers, increasing the chance of success
> - Competition may be limited by the franchisor restricting other outlets in the same area
> - Supplier relationships are already established by the franchisor
> 
> AO2
> 
> - An established brand means customers already trust the product, making it easier to attract sales from day one and reducing the risk of failure
> - Shared marketing costs reduce the individual franchisee's expenses while still providing national or wider coverage
> - Support from the franchisor is particularly valuable to someone new to business ownership, reducing the risk of costly mistakes
> - A known product or service builds a customer base more quickly than an unknown start-up business
> - Restricted competition gives the franchisee a protected market, helping to maintain stable revenue
> - Ready-made supplier relationships can mean better prices and a more reliable supply chain from the outset
> 
> Other valid chains of reasoning are acceptable.

parts.problem_md: Explain **two **advantages to a business of being a social enterprise.
parts.solution_md:
One advantage of being a social enterprise is that it may attract more customers, as the business is seen as ethical and community-focused **[1]**. Customers who share these values are more likely to choose it over a profit-driven competitor **[1]**

A second advantage is that employees may be easier to recruit and retain **[1]**. People motivated by social values are drawn to working for social enterprises, reducing recruitment costs **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Explain requires a clear statement of meaning (AO1) supported by contextual development (AO2)
> 
> - Valid AO1 is awarded 2 marks
> - Valid AO2 is awarded up to 2 marks
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> AO1
> 
> - May attract more customers because the business is seen as ethical and community-focused
> - Customers may be willing to pay a higher price than they would to a profit-driven competitor
> - Employees may be easier to recruit, as people are drawn to working for a social enterprise
> - Employees may be easier to retain, leading to lower labour turnover
> - Government grants or subsidies may be available
> 
> AO2
> 
> - Being seen as ethical increases demand for the product or service, boosting sales and revenue
> - A higher price increases revenue and profit margin without needing to attract more customers
> - Lower recruitment costs and a larger pool of motivated candidates improve the quality of the workforce
> - Lower labour turnover reduces the cost of recruiting and training replacements, and maintains consistency of service
> - Grants or subsidies reduce costs, freeing up funds to invest in the business or its social mission
> 
> Other valid chains of reasoning are acceptable.

> **[exam-tip]**
> Make sure you develop each advantage fully rather than simply listing them. A clear explanation means you identify the advantage and then link it to a positive outcome for the business - e.g. stating that a social enterprise attracts customers is only partial; explaining that this increases sales revenue makes it a clear explanation. Two well-developed points are needed for full marks, so aim to write a brief chain of reasoning for each advantage. Avoid repeating the same point in different words, as this will only be credited once.

parts.problem_md: Define the term 'franchise'.
parts.solution_md:
A franchise is a business arrangement where the owner of a brand (the franchisor) allows another person or company (the franchisee) to trade using its brand name, products and systems **[1]**, in exchange for an initial fee and ongoing royalty payments **[1]**

parts.problem_md: Analyse **two** reasons why a sole trader might choose to become a private limited company.
parts.solution_md:
One reason a sole trader might choose to become a private limited company is to gain limited liability **[K]**. As a sole trader, the owner has unlimited liability, meaning personal assets such as their home and savings are at risk if the business accumulates debts it cannot pay **[An]**. By incorporating, the owner can only lose the amount they have invested in the company. This significantly reduces the personal financial risk of running the business and may make the owner more willing to take calculated risks, such as expanding into new markets or investing in new equipment, that they might previously have avoided out of fear of losing personal assets **[An]**. As a result, incorporation can open up growth opportunities that are simply too risky to pursue as a sole trader **[An]**

A second reason is to make it easier to raise finance **[K]**. A sole trader cannot sell shares and must rely on personal savings or bank loans to fund the business, which limits how much capital they can access. By becoming a private limited company, the owner can sell shares to family, friends or private investors, providing a much larger pool of finance **[An]**. Unlike a bank loan, this does not create debt or require interest payments, which means the additional capital can be invested directly into growing the business - for example, by purchasing new equipment or hiring additional staff - without reducing profitability **[An]**. This makes incorporation particularly attractive to a sole trader who wants to expand but has exhausted their personal sources of finance **[An]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> - An 8-mark analyse question requires two developed points, each with knowledge of a relevant concept, followed by a chain of reasoning that explains the causes, impacts or consequences
> - This is a 'Level of response' answer where the examiner judges how well you have displayed the key skills of knowledge, understanding and analysis
> 
> | **Level** | **Marks** | **Descriptor** |
> |---|---|---|
> | **4** | 7-8 | - Good analysis of the reasons why a sole trader might choose to become a private limited company |
> |   |   |   |
> | **3** | 5-6 | - Limited analysis of the reasons why a sole trader might choose to become a private limited company |
> | **2** | 3-4 | - Application of the reasons why a sole trader might choose to become a private limited company |
> | **1** | 1 -2 | - Knowledge and understanding of a sole trader and/or private limited company |
> |   |   |   |
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> - A sole trader has unlimited liability, meaning personal assets such as their home and savings are at risk if the business cannot pay its debts. By incorporating, the owner gains limited liability and can only lose the amount they have invested in the company. This significantly reduces personal financial risk and may encourage the owner to take calculated risks that they would have been too cautious to attempt as a sole trader
> - A sole trader cannot sell shares to raise finance and must rely on personal savings, bank loans or personal investment; by becoming a private limited company, the owner can sell shares to family, friends or private investors, accessing a much larger pool of capital. This finance can be used to fund expansion without taking on debt, avoiding interest payments that would reduce the business's profitability and making growth more financially sustainable
> - Incorporation gives the business a separate legal identity, meaning the company can continue to exist if the owner becomes ill or dies. This provides continuity that is not possible for a sole trader, protecting customers, employees and the value of the business from the disruption that would occur if it ceased to exist due to the owner's death or incapacity
> - A private limited company may be seen as more credible and established than a sole trader, making it easier to win contracts, attract investment and negotiate favourable terms with suppliers - none of which are as easily achieved when operating as an unincorporated business
> 
> Other valid chains of reasoning are acceptable.

> **[exam-tip]**
> Many students lose marks on "Analyse" questions by simply identifying reasons without developing them. Make sure each reason follows a clear chain of argument: state the reason, apply it to a realistic business situation, and then explain the consequences or impact on the business.
> 
> A useful technique is to use connective phrases such as "this means that…", "as a result…" or "therefore…" to signal that you are moving from description into analysis. Aim to write two well-developed paragraphs rather than listing several undeveloped points.
> 
> Avoid spending time on evaluation (e.g. weighing up whether incorporation is the best option overall) - the command word is "Analyse", not "Evaluate", so marks are awarded for depth of reasoning rather than judgement.

parts.problem_md: Explain **one **reason why a business might remain a private limited company rather than change to a public limited company.
parts.solution_md:
One reason a business might stay private rather than become a plc is that the owners do not want to lose control **[1]**. If shares are sold to the general public, new shareholders may buy up a large number of shares, which reduces the original owners' ownership and voting power **[1]**. This means the owners could end up losing the ability to make important decisions without needing approval from outside shareholders, which may stop them running the business the way they originally intended **[1]**

> - Valid AO2 is awarded up to 2 marks

> 
> AO1
> 
> - Does not want to lose control - selling shares to the general public risks diluting the current owners' ownership
> - Does not want the cost and complexity of floating on a stock exchange
> - Does not want to publish accounts or face increased public scrutiny
> - Already has sufficient sources of finance (e.g. venture capital) so there is no need to go public
> - May not be ready to float - for example, if the business is making losses
> - Wants to retain the business's distinctive values, culture or family ownership
> - Current shareholders may be willing to accept postponed dividend payments, reducing pressure to list
> 
> AO2
>

> - The process of listing on a stock exchange involves significant legal and administrative costs, as well as management time that could be spent running the business
> - Publishing accounts means competitors can access detailed financial information, potentially undermining the business's competitive position
> - If finance needs are already being met, the risks and costs of going public - including loss of control and increased scrutiny - outweigh any benefits
> - If the business is making losses, a stock market listing could undervalue it or fail to attract enough investors
> - Once listed, pressure from shareholders for short-term profits may conflict with the long-term values or family culture the owners want to preserve

One reason for AC to convert to a plc is to raise the large amounts of capital needed to fund its planned expansion **[K]**. parts.problem_md: Analyse **two **disadvantages to a sole trader of changing to a partnership.
parts.solution_md:
One disadvantage of changing to a partnership is that the sole trader loses sole control of decision-making **[K]**. Previously, they could make all decisions independently and act quickly when opportunities or problems arose. Once partners join the business, agreement must be reached before decisions can be made **[An]**. If the partners have different views on how the business should be run, this can cause conflict and slow down the decision-making process considerably **[An]**. As a result, the business may miss time-sensitive opportunities that it would previously have been able to act on quickly, weakening its competitive position **[An]**

Also, each partner is legally liable for the actions of all other partners **[K]**. This means that if one partner takes on a large debt or signs an expensive contract without the others' consent, all partners are equally responsible for that obligation **[An]**. For the original sole trader, this represents a significant new risk - previously they were only answerable for their own decisions, but now a partner's poor judgement could expose them to unlimited liability for debts they played no part in creating **[An]**. In the worst case, this could put their personal assets, such as their home or savings, at risk **[An]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> - An 8-mark analyse question requires two developed points, each with knowledge of a relevant concept, followed by a chain of reasoning that explains the causes, impacts or consequences
> - This is a 'Level of response' answer where the examiner judges how well you have displayed the key skills of knowledge, understanding and analysis
> 
> | **Level** | **Marks** | **Descriptor** |
> |---|---|---|
> | **4** | 7-8 | - Good analysis of the disadvantages to a sole trader of changing to a partnership |
> |   |   |   |
> | **3** | 5-6 | - Limited analysis of the disadvantages to a sole trader of changing to a partnership |
> | **2** | 3-4 | - Application of the disadvantages to a sole trader of changing to a partnership |
> | **1** | 1 -2 | - Knowledge and understanding of sole trader or partnership |
> |   |   |   |
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> - When a sole trader changes to a partnership, they lose sole control and must share decision-making with the new partner(s). Previously, the sole trader could act quickly and independently; now, agreement must be reached before decisions can be made. If the partners have different views on the direction of the business, this can cause conflict and significantly slow down decision-making, meaning the business may miss opportunities that require a fast response
> - In a partnership, each partner is legally bound by the actions of all other partners. If one partner takes on a large debt or signs an expensive contract without the others' consent, all partners are equally liable for that obligation. This is a significant risk for the original sole trader, who previously only had to answer for their own decisions - a partner's poor judgement could expose all partners to unlimited liability, putting their personal assets at risk
> - Changing to a partnership means profits must be shared between all partners. Previously, the sole trader kept all of the profit they generated; now, a portion goes to the new partner(s), reducing the original owner's financial reward even if their contribution to the business has not changed. This could reduce the sole trader's motivation, particularly if they feel they are working just as hard for a smaller return
> 
> Other valid chains of reasoning are acceptable.
